findings.claim: Fourteen Easy plates from the Path's opening semesters
findings.because: The brief's items give The French Omelette difficulty 2 (the library's Intermediate), so only thirteen of the fourteen are Easy plates; and five of the fourteen (Crêpes, Panna Cotta, Pad Krapow Moo, Bulgogi, Rau Muong Xao Toi) sit in semesters 6 and 8, which are not the Path's opening semesters. The omelette is placed here by its semester, not its difficulty.
findings.fix: Fourteen plates, most of them Easy and most from the Path's opening semesters, each one technique deep, cooked and logged before you move on.

findings.claim: take The French Omelette before anything else: eight minutes, and the whole of heat control and seasoning in one pan
findings.because: The brief marks the omelette difficulty 2, the only plate at this level that is not Easy. The order can stand (its semester says it is where every cook begins) but a commis should be told it is the hardest plate here, or they will read a failed omelette as a failure of the level.
findings.fix: take The French Omelette before anything else, knowing it is the one Intermediate plate at this level: eight minutes, and the whole of heat control and seasoning in one pan

findings.claim: because it is the busiest plate at this level
findings.because: The brief lists four techniques for Chicken Piccata and four for Bulgogi (knife cuts, marinating, rendering fat, searing), so piccata is not the busiest plate at the level, only the busiest of its semester.
findings.fix: because it is the busiest of the four

findings.claim: By the third of these, the semester's four moves, sear, deglaze, mount, plate, should be in your hands.
findings.because: None of the three placed dishes lists mounting in its techniques (Shrimp Scampi: deglazing and searing; Chicken Teriyaki: resting and slicing; Garides Saganaki: flambé, keeping the cooking liquid, sweating), so the primer promises a move that no item here teaches. The four moves are the semester's blurb, not this level's dishes.
findings.fix: By the third of these, sear, deglaze and plate should be in your hands; the mount is the semester's fourth move, and none of these three teaches it.

findings.claim: each is a pan or a pot you will be handed in your first weeks
findings.because: The standard's own text puts the wok among the Level III techniques whose standard governs a whole service, and the flambé pan of Garides Saganaki is not a first-weeks pan either; paragraph 4 itself says five dishes sit further up the Path. "Each" overstates it.

findings.claim: They ask for a braise, a bread or a custard held to a standard

findings.claim: Salted water & the float test, the bare simmer and blanching & shocking are one lesson at three heats
findings.because: Two of the three run at the same heat. The brief's marks for salted water want a pot that "returns to its boil quickly after the food goes in and never stops moving", and blanching wants "a large volume at a hard rolling boil"; only the bare simmer sits below the boil. Two heats, not three.

findings.claim: learn which before anything else here

findings.claim: are dry heat at three distances
findings.because: Distance is not what separates them: the brief's charring standard names "flame, a broiler, or bare hot metal" as charring's own heat, and roasting is "dry ambient heat in an enclosed oven" while the broiler is "top-down radiant heat". What differs is where the heat comes from.
findings.fix: are dry heat from three directions: all around, from above, and straight against the surface

findings.claim: come down to full commitment, then drying the surface before heat
findings.because: "Fully committed either way" is brining & curing's mark alone. Salting to draw the water out is met on different marks: salted evenly over every surface, laid out so the water has somewhere to go (a colander, a rack, a sieve over a bowl), visible liquid to show for it, and that liquid squeezed, blotted or poured away. As written the reader would salt and wait and never pour the water off.
findings.fix: come down to salt on every face, somewhere for the water to go, that water poured off, and the surface dry before heat

findings.claim: work down it in the order above

findings.claim: Chuck wins at braising because hard-working muscle melts into gelatin low, slow and wet, and fights you fast.
findings.because: Muscle does not melt into gelatin; collagen does. The brief's Chuck entry says it plainly: "cook it low, slow, and wet and the collagen melts into gelatin", and the register sample says the same of braising ("its connective tissue melts into gelatin"). A cook who repeats "muscle melts" at the pass is wrong.
findings.fix: Chuck wins at braising because its connective tissue melts into gelatin low, slow and wet, and it fights you fast.

findings.claim: the Repair Table gives the levers in order of gentleness: salt first, then acid, then umami.
findings.because: That is the Repair Table's fix for TOO FLAT only ("salt first; if salted, acid; if bright, umami"). The other fault placed at Level I is salty, and its levers are different: "dilute (unsalted liquid, more base), bulk (starch, cream), or counter (acid and a touch of sugar)". As written, a cook reads salt as the first lever for a salty dish.
findings.fix: the Repair Table gives each its levers in order of gentleness: for flat, salt first, then acid, then umami; for salty, dilute, bulk or counter.

findings.claim: Poach, Simmer, Boil are three temperatures pretending to be one method; Blanch & Shock is how a green vegetable prepped at noon plates at eight. Knife Cuts: The Classical Ladder gives the dice and the julienne their sizes
findings.because: The order is unsound for a Commis: the cuts come after five pan verbs, yet "cook the onions" assumes the onion is already diced, and the Mirepoix entry's base is "cut small" before it is cooked in fat. Knife Cuts sits in the same Knife & Prep group as Mise en Place with the same semester 1. A knife cut belongs before the dish that needs it.
findings.fix: Take Mise en Place first, because everything else assumes it: read fully, prep completely, then light the burner. Knife Cuts: The Classical Ladder comes next, before anything hits a pan: it gives the dice and the julienne their sizes and says what matters now: uniformity, not speed. Then the pan verbs, because a recipe says cook the onions and means one of three things. (Then continue with Sweat vs. Sauté vs. Sear through Blanch & Shock, dropping the Knife Cuts sentence from its present place.)

findings.claim: because the family entry gives the rule and the single entry gives the exception.

Telling a cook every single entry is an exception misreads three of four.
findings.fix: because the family entry gives the rule and the single entry gives the particulars, and sometimes the exception.

findings.claim: Braised and Roasted are the slow ones.

The brief's own Roasted card says only "Cooked by dry heat in an oven until browned outside and tender inside" and contrasts it with braising because "no liquid goes in", and the Rack of Lamb card says the rack "is roasted fast and hot". problems.issue: Paragraph 3 ends: "By the third of these, three of the semester's four moves should be in your hands: sear, deglaze, plate. The mount is the fourth, and none of these three teaches it." That is wrong. The Shrimp Scampi recipe (src/lib/data/recipes.full.json) has the step "Mount with butter, add lemon; return shrimp 1 min to finish" and its note says "The sauce itself is a butter mount: wine reduced, then cold butter swirled in off the heat." A cook told the scampi does not teach the mount will be corrected at the pass.
problems.fix: Rewrite the two sentences so the scampi carries the mount. Replace "Shrimp Scampi repeats the sear and the deglaze from the piccata" with "Shrimp Scampi repeats the sear and the deglaze from the piccata and adds the mount, cold butter swirled into the reduced wine off the heat", and replace the last two sentences of the paragraph with "By the third of these, the semester's four moves should be in your hands: sear, deglaze, mount, plate." Nothing else in the primer changes.

problems.issue: Paragraph 3 says "Salmon, Tuna, Swordfish and Halibut each carry a doneness note" and "braised Short Rib has no temperature to ask for". critic.notes: Things the operator may want, none of them a primer fault. (1) The Level test sentence (untimed, across the subsections, ends on what you missed with the right answers) appears near-verbatim in six of the eight primers (dishes, lexicon, plates, palate, safety, service) because every brief carries a levelTest field; on one level page that is the same sentence six times. If the level page states it once at the foot, the primers could drop it, or the field could be marked as already shown. (2) Service module 2 (srv-allergens) is met through its one term, \"Food Safety: The Chef-Owner's Non-Negotiables\", but that term is not among the 266 Level I Lexicon items; the drill uses the whole track as its field so nothing is barred, but the module sits at Level I while its only term appears to be placed higher in the Lexicon. Worth a look at the placement. (3) The Plates brief lists only three of the five corrections for Culinary Spices and for The World of Culinary Mushrooms (getsWrong is truncated to three); the plates primer handled it honestly (\"three of them are these\"), but an author cannot check the other two. (4) Minor and not flagged as a problem: the techniques primer says knife cuts \"sit on more recipes than almost anything else here\" (150); sweating (198), salted water (188) and the bare simmer (183) carry more, so it is defensible but loose. (5) Verified as correct and left alone: every technique mark quoted in the techniques primer, the deck's 20 methods and 9 language cards, the lexicon's 61 vegetables and 25 cuts, the Chuck and honing definitions, the repair table's \"in order of gentleness\", all four plate correction counts, the service outcomes, and every name in every next line against neighbours.above.
